chapters.title: Influences
chapters.hook: Why does the clean desk lose to a glowing news tab before breakfast?
chapters.counterintuition: A person can mean every promise and still lose to repeated inputs. The feed, the friend group, and the messy closet get a vote before discipline speaks.
chapters.tryThisNow: The next time you feel the pull to open a feed, do not tap yet. Write: "Not now; I choose the input I want."
chapters.keyTakeaway: You compound better choices by designing your inputs: trim noisy information, choose wiser associations, seek mentors, and clear clutter so good action is easier to repeat.

breakdown.fastRead:
Hailey's news tab is half loaded when the class mood changes. One muttered headline turns a room into a worry loop. The tiny click came first. Influence design means choosing the inputs, people, and spaces that shape you while you are busy. Inputs become instructions when they repeat.

You do not fix every habit by trying harder. You lower the force pushing against it. Guard the feed. Aim the commute. Choose closer voices. Clear the space that keeps calling you back.
breakdown.deepRead:
One small input can steer the next hour before you notice. A headline makes your shoulders tighten. A podcast puts a useful idea in reach. A friend normalizes the missed workout. A pile by the door keeps whispering that you are behind.

Your brain is an information-processing machine in the plain sense: it works with what you keep feeding it. An Information Diet is not about hiding from the world. It is about refusing to make low-grade news and media the first meal of your attention. If the morning starts with outrage, the next choice has to climb out of a hole.

Drive-Time University uses the same gear in a better way. Bryce does not find a secret extra hour. He takes a route he already drives and fills it with audiobooks or courses instead of loose noise. The car was shaping him either way. Now the input has a job.

The social channel works the same way, but it feels more personal. The Association audit starts from a blunt 95% success-or-failure claim: friends, mentors and advisers can help set what feels normal. That does not mean coldly ranking people. It means asking who makes the next good choice cheaper. Better company makes better choices cheaper.
breakdown.fullRead:
Hazel pulls one envelope from the closet because the door will not shut. She expects hangers. She finds a renewal notice, then the fee she would have canceled if the paper had not vanished into the tote. Clutter Cleanup is not just neatness. Your room votes before you do.

Influence design can sound cold if you hear only the word control. The better read is care for your future attention. You are not a sealed box making pure choices. You are a body in a room, a thumb near a feed, a driver with audio running, and a friend shaped by the group chat that keeps lighting up.

Start with information. The Information Diet asks what you are letting in through news and media. If it keeps you scared, scattered, or angry before your own work begins, it is not neutral. Replace some of it with better instruction, or leave the gap quiet enough for your own thought to return.

Drive-Time University is the gentler proof. Bryce does not become a new person because the dashboard plays a course. He removes one common leak. The same road that used to feed filler now feeds audiobooks or courses. Small inputs gain force because the route keeps coming back.

Then look at associations. The audit is not a license to abandon every loved one who does not share your goal. Quantity and quality can change without contempt. Janet may spend less time in a draining loop and still make the time warmer, cleaner, and more honest. She can also seek mentors and advisers who have already reached the place she wants to go.

New peers help for the same reason. A goal feels less strange when someone nearby already talks that way. You borrow norms before you borrow tactics. That can work against you in a cynical group, and it can work for you in a group that expects follow-through.

Finally, look at environment. Physical clutter pulls with objects: the form, the bill, the box by the door. Mental clutter pulls with open loops: the unresolved message, the half-made choice, the old material that keeps poisoning the mood. The aim is lower friction. A cleaner space does not make you noble. It makes the next useful act easier to start.

Where this breaks is any case where the input is not yours to choose. A caregiver in a noisy clinic, a worker under a harsh boss, or a student in an unsafe home cannot solve the problem by playing a better audiobook. If the rent, school, or shift controls the influence, the next move is help, protection, or negotiation. Influence design works best when it gives you a real handle, not when it blames you for a room you cannot leave.

examples.title: Tab Before Class
examples.scenario: "Another headline before the quiz," someone mutters near the teacher's desk, and teacher Hailey stops scrolling. Her news and media tab is still loading beside the Information Diet handout. The room has become an information-processing machine for panic before the lesson begins. Hailey catches the error mid-click: she is feeding the mood she meant to steady, and the next click will set the class's first input.
examples.whatToDo: Hailey closes the tab before it loads, names the mistake to herself, and opens the clean lesson file that matches the input she wants the room to carry.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery starts at the moment of noticing. If you catch the input while it is still entering, you can stop feeding the state you are trying to change.

examples.title: Route Audio
examples.scenario: "Stay on this route," the navigation voice says, and rideshare driver Bryce hovers over the same morning clips. The airport queue creeps forward. He thinks this is not real reading time, then Drive-Time University needles him: audiobooks and courses count because the road is already here. Quiet, noise, excuse, course. His thumb rests on the play button before the car moves.
examples.whatToDo: Bryce queues one course before the next ride request, using the route as the cue instead of waiting for a perfect reading chair.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene turns a stale time block into a learning input. The road does not have to become empty time just because printed reading is not possible.

examples.title: Hour Before Sleep
examples.scenario: The direct-message thread full of complaints sits above an unread note from a mentor, and both want Brandon's evening. He is on the bedroom floor with the phone charging, planning the only free hour before sleep. The Association audit has made the 95% success-or-failure claim hard to ignore: friends, mentors and advisers all count as inputs. No action yet; he is allotting attention before the night spends it for him.
examples.whatToDo: Brandon should assign the hour before opening either thread, giving the mentor note a defined place instead of letting the loudest chat spend his attention.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning is the move here. Influence design starts before contact, when you still have a chance to choose which relationship gets the scarce attention.

examples.title: Clipboard Window
examples.scenario: The regular line captain is home sick, so volunteer Janet gets the clipboard during the Saturday pickup shift while the food bank line presses against the taped floor. Her oldest friend is waiting after shift for their usual long complaint loop. A mentor has offered the same narrow window to talk about the job Janet wants. She is torn between a friend she loves and a mentor window she may not get back. The Association audit and its 95% success-or-failure claim make both paths sting.
examples.whatToDo: Janet should keep care in the friendship while changing the shape: a shorter, warmer check-in now, then the mentor call during the rare open window.
examples.whyItMatters: The hard edge is not crude rejection. Quality can preserve a tie while quantity shifts toward people who help make the next good choice more normal.

examples.title: Renewal In The Chair
examples.scenario: Client Presley taps the storage-app renewal invoice at Chantal's salon during her lunch appointment while the cape snaps at her collar. "It is just one more month," she says from the chair. Chantal parts her hair. "For the boxes or for the worry?" Presley sees the card fee. "Both." Chantal nods. "Then Clutter Cleanup starts with the thing charging you." Presley looks at the physical clutter photo and the mental clutter on the bill.
examples.whatToDo: Presley should pause the renewal, choose the first box to sort, and stop letting a hidden monthly charge make the old clutter feel harmless.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange makes the cost visible. Clutter is not only what takes space; it is also what keeps sending claims on money, time, and attention.

examples.title: Door That Would Not Shut
examples.scenario: The bedroom closet door sticks on a bulging tote, and Hazel expects the Clutter Cleanup to be about hangers. She tugs one receipt envelope free so the door can close. The envelope brings a health form, then an unpaid renewal notice, then the charge she would have canceled if she had seen it. The physical clutter is now mental clutter with a fee attached, and one tiny pull has exposed the chain.
examples.whatToDo: Hazel should follow the chain instead of restuffing the tote: handle the renewal, make one home for active papers, and clear the cue that keeps reopening.
examples.whyItMatters: One small act cascades because clutter links objects to open loops. Clearing one stuck place can reveal the real behavior cost hiding behind it.

questions.prompt: You want to improve an evening habit and start by ranking friends, while the phone feed and room stay unchanged. Which audit fits influence design?
choices: Review the friend group first, since social pressure is the main input that matters.
Check the information, associations, and environment that keep feeding the habit.
Write a stronger goal first, since surroundings only matter after motivation drops.
questions.explanation: Influence design uses three channels: information, associations, and environment. Friends matter, but a feed and a room can shape the habit too.

questions.prompt: A worker says the morning news cannot affect behavior because the real choice happens later at the desk. Which reply matches the information section?
choices: Change the input quality, since the brain works with what it repeatedly receives.
Keep the intake separate, since behavior starts after the reading or watching ends.
Balance each bad item with a good item, since volume matters more than source quality.
questions.explanation: The information section makes intake part of the behavior system. If the brain processes what enters it, low-quality input is not separate from later action.

questions.prompt: Your first break keeps disappearing into angry clips and headline hopping. Which change best matches guarding against garbage?
choices: Track how long the media takes, since short bursts leave attention mostly untouched.
Cut the low-quality news and media that keep crowding the goal from attention.
Keep the media but repeat the goal after it, since awareness cancels the input.
questions.explanation: Guarding against garbage means reducing repeated news and media that crowd attention. Knowing your goal does not make the input neutral.

questions.prompt: A commuter says learning will begin once there is quiet seated reading time. Which response follows Drive-Time University?
choices: Save learning for seated reading, because audio may make the commute feel less restful.
Use the commute for quiet only, because travel time sits outside learning time.
Put audiobooks or courses into the route, because the listening block already exists.
questions.explanation: Drive-Time University turns travel and routine listening into learning inputs. It does not wait for a perfect reading chair before instruction can start.

questions.prompt: After hearing the 95% success-or-failure claim, a team lead says friends are only emotional support. What correction fits the claim?
choices: Treat surrounding people as outcome-shaping norms, not just a comfort system.
Treat surrounding people as morale help, while results come from private effort.
Treat surrounding people as optional once the goal and plan are clear.
questions.explanation: The claim gives associations a direct role in outcomes. Support matters, but the group also shapes norms, expectations, and tolerated behavior.

questions.prompt: A coordinator has the same weekly calls, but each one leaves the target habit feeling foolish. Which Association audit question comes first?
choices: Give each current tie the same time so the audit does not create tension.
Ask which ties support and inspire the target, then adjust exposure.
Keep the longest friendships central so history carries more weight than direction.
questions.explanation: The audit asks whether nearby people support and inspire the direction. Equal time can keep a draining norm in place, even when the goal is clear.

questions.prompt: You worry influence design sounds like abandoning a loved one who is not goal-aligned. Which response keeps the hard edge?
choices: Replace the relationship quickly with goal-aligned peers so the signal stays clean.
Keep the same amount of time to prove the person still matters to you.
Use less quantity with more care so the connection can stay intact.
questions.explanation: The unit allows quality-focused limits. The answer is not blanket rejection or unchanged exposure; it is more intentional contact with less drag.

questions.prompt: A designer wants a mentor and has three options. Which choice best fits the mentor standard in this unit?
choices: Choose the likable person who gives fast encouragement after every setback.
Choose the friend with similar goals so both learn from the same place.
Choose someone further along the path who can share patterns and warnings.
questions.explanation: Mentors and advisers are tied to the future position you want. Likability and shared struggle may help, but relevant distance ahead is the key test.

questions.prompt: A renter cleans the desk but keeps a pile of unpaid forms and old angry messages beside the bed. Which environment read is right?
choices: Remove the physical and mental clutter that keeps pulling attention off course.
Clean only the visible room, since environment means the space in front of you.
Work on focus first, since clutter matters only after the task has begun.
questions.explanation: Environment includes physical and mental clutter. A room is only one part; unfinished and poisonous material can keep pulling behavior away.

reviewCards.front: What are the three influence channels this unit asks you to audit?
reviewCards.back: Audit information, associations, and environment. Each channel keeps sending cues before you make a formal choice, so each one can make a habit easier or harder.

reviewCards.front: Why is the Information Diet more than a mood tip?
reviewCards.back: It treats the brain as an information-processing machine. The quality of news, media, and other inputs affects the thoughts you have ready when it is time to act.

reviewCards.front: How does Drive-Time University turn dead time into compound input?
reviewCards.back: It puts audiobooks or courses into travel and waiting blocks that already exist. The time is not created; the input inside it is changed.

reviewCards.front: What mistake does the association audit avoid with loved ones?
reviewCards.back: It avoids crude abandonment. Some relationships may need less quantity and more quality, so connection stays while exposure to the draining pattern shrinks.

reviewCards.front: How can clutter influence behavior when no one else is present?
reviewCards.back: Physical clutter keeps objects in the way, and mental clutter keeps open loops in attention. Both can pull you back toward the old behavior.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more when a repeated input keeps breaking your rhythm, behavioral momentum (Ch 4) or influence design, and why?
reviewCards.back: Change the input first. Momentum can carry a routine after it starts, but a noisy feed or draining room can knock the routine off course before it gains force.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching the input before it becomes the mood. Run the Input Gate by naming which channel is active: information, associations, or environment. Then make one small change to what enters next.

ifThenPlans.context: If a feed starts filling your first break with news and media
ifThenPlans.plan: If the feed is shaping the break, then run the Input Gate. Close it and choose one input that helps the next task.

ifThenPlans.context: If a commute or errand line will happen anyway
ifThenPlans.plan: If the route is open audio time, then run the Input Gate. Queue an audiobook or course before loose noise fills the space.

ifThenPlans.context: If a familiar thread keeps turning into a draining loop
ifThenPlans.plan: If the relationship matters but the pattern drains you, then run the Input Gate. Offer a shorter, warmer contact instead of the long loop.

ifThenPlans.context: If one pile or open loop keeps calling from your space
ifThenPlans.plan: If the room keeps voting for delay, then run the Input Gate. Remove the cue or make one clear home for the active item.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, pre-write one refusal before the first low-quality input you catch: "No feed now; I choose ___." Fill the blank with the better input.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, change one thing in your setup: remove a news shortcut, add a course link, or clear one active paper tray. Watch which input you reach for first.

memorableLines.text: Inputs become instructions when they repeat.
Better company makes better choices cheaper.
Your room votes before you do.

chapters.title: Acceleration
chapters.hook: Your 5-to-6 extra reps come after the clean form runs out.
chapters.counterintuition: Despite its name, acceleration makes you pay at the hard spot: more effort, more thought, more care. When the usual path stalls, that added push separates you from the average stop.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next task handoff, touch your laptop lid and write one demand you can remove, then label the extra effort the space will fund.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Momentum hits a wall before acceleration begins. Add one smart push with extra energy, Obstacle Leverage, or expectation-plus, and use the place most people stop.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why does Tobias quit when the gym gets loud and the hard set begins? He came in with momentum, then the clean reps run out and the next weight feels like proof he has found his ceiling. Acceleration starts in that pause. The easy days were the warm-up. The hard spot is the hinge.

You do not fake progress. You add a smart push after honest effort has reached a wall. The 3 levers are extra energy, obstacle leverage, and expectation-plus. Use more care, use the obstacle as the test, or add value after the baseline is met. Walls test the work. When most people stop at the same rough edge, one added rep, one better question, or one extra bit of care can change the result.
breakdown.deepRead:
Pressure sorts effort that looked equal on easy days. Two runners can keep the same plan while the road is flat. The hill shows who owns the plan and who only enjoyed the glide.

Arnold Schwarzenegger's cheat reps make the edge plain. At a weight lifting limit, strict form stopped giving him reps. He did not pretend the wall was fake. He adjusted the movement enough to bring in more muscle groups and add five to six extra reps. A detour is honest when it keeps you working.

The order matters. Momentum first, adjustment second. If you bend the work before strain appears, you are only making it easy. If you adjust after a true stop, the change can keep the set alive. That is the line between a shortcut and a smart detour.

Expectation-plus works the same way outside the gym. You finish the promised report, then add the plain next step that saves the other person a round of guessing. You answer the customer, then include the setup they will need tomorrow. You meet the bar, then add one useful bit of care. The extra is small, but it lands where the result is still soft.

You can feel the cost right there. Extra energy is not a mood. It is the second pass when the first pass was enough to avoid blame. Obstacle leverage is not liking the hard part. It is reading the hard part as the place where the work starts to matter. Expectation-plus is not showing off. It is adding value after competence has already been reached.
breakdown.fullRead:
Sarah's draft is good enough to send, so why does the last pass feel expensive? The file meets the request. The message has no typos. The video-call waiting room is already open. The ordinary move is to click send and call it done.

Acceleration asks a sharper question: what would change the outcome now that the baseline is safe? Sometimes the answer is one more sentence that names the next step. Sometimes it is a shorter path through an obstacle. Sometimes it is one extra lift after the honest set is over. The move may be brief, but it is not free. Someone must carry that added cost before the benefit shows.

Obstacle Leverage gives the hard spot a job. The easy stretch was the warm-up, and real growth begins when the plan has to meet pressure. Most people meet a version of the same hill: the blank chart before a call, the dead phone before a trip, the customer reply that needs care after the promised fix. If everyone faces a rough edge, the edge becomes a place to separate. Average behavior stops where relief starts.

This is where acceleration can be misused. It is not a reason to cram more into every hour. A tired parent, a sick body, or a wrong goal may need rest or a changed plan, not another push. The source idea has an order: effort has been steady, momentum exists, and the goal still matters. Then the obstacle is a signal to add something smarter.

Watch the order in real life. Mathias promised himself he would be a person who practiced Expectation-Plus Effort, then the bowling league check-in ran long and the easy thing was to meet expectations only in speech. He cut the add-on contest, walked first-timers through scoring, and left the closing clerk a clean handoff note. His stated value met a cost. He had to give up a small bit of show to exceed expectations with useful care.

That trade is the price. You give up the neat ending where competence is enough. You give up one lesser demand so the better effort has room. You give up the comfort of saying the wall proves you are done. Extra effort has a bill.

Sarah feels that bill at the end of her draft. The waiting room is open, and the file could go. Instead she removes one optional paragraph, writes the next step in plain words, and sends a shorter, kinder note. No one claps. She is late to the easy version of done. But the person on the other side knows what to do next, and Sarah has kept the promise that mattered.

examples.title: Locker-Room Reset
examples.scenario: Tobias's palm stops halfway to the towel hook beside the gym front desk, while the bar still burns in his forearms. He had promised strict-form sets, but the last clean lift died at his weight lifting limit. Arnold Schwarzenegger's cheat-rep lesson gives him a restart: do not fake the set, adjust after the true stop. Tobias drops the towel, resets his stance, and works for five to six extra reps.
examples.whatToDo: Tobias pauses before ending the session. He treats the failed clean rep as the limit, then restarts with a controlled adjustment that keeps work moving.
examples.whyItMatters: Arnold's example protects the hard edge. A smart detour comes after real effort reaches a wall, not before effort gets uncomfortable.

examples.title: One-Percent Hallway
examples.scenario: Sliding the laundry basket with one knee, Cyrus bumps the hallway wall and hears his phone chirp low battery. The charger is in the car, his ride is outside, and the packing streak that felt easy all week is suddenly thin. He names the snag Obstacle Leverage, not a ruined plan. The basket stays down, the boarding pass opens, and the hard minute becomes the part that counts.
examples.whatToDo: Cyrus stops treating the snag as an insult to the plan. He handles the one action the trip now needs before he returns to the basket.
examples.whyItMatters: Easy consistency was only the warm-up. The obstacle shows whether the routine can protect the result when the smooth part ends.

examples.title: Renewal After Delay
examples.scenario: Lawrence's lunch was interrupted by the renewal notice after the support delay had already been settled. The log later made the path visible: his first reply did enough to meet expectations, then he added a call, a setup note, and one clean next step in the reply-all email. That Expectation-Plus Effort did not erase the delay. It showed how added care can exceed expectations.
examples.whatToDo: Lawrence studies the record for the added care, not just the deadline. He keeps the call, setup note, and next step in the recovery playbook.
examples.whyItMatters: Meeting expectations can stop the bleeding. Exceeding them can rebuild trust because the other person feels the extra thought.

examples.title: Waiting-Room Catch
examples.scenario: There is no time to rebuild the slide deck before the video-call waiting room fills, and project lead Asher feels it with the trackpad warm under his wrist. He promised to arrive prepared, but the one chart he needs is still blank. Halfway through a frantic search, he catches his own mistake: the easy work was only warm-up, and more tabs will not save him. Obstacle Leverage means using the squeeze for real growth.
examples.whatToDo: Asher names the search as the error while it is happening. He drops the weak section and turns the obstacle into one defensible answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The useful moment is the noticing. Acceleration starts when pressure redirects effort toward the next honest move instead of more motion.

examples.title: Bowling Memo Cut
examples.scenario: Every lane in the bowling league was booked, and the staff plan only covered check-in. Mathias wrote the manager memo before sending it: Baseline to meet expectations: open desk, rented shoes, posted lane list. Acceleration to exceed expectations: cut the add-on contest, walk first-timers through scoring, and leave the closing clerk one cleaned handoff note. Expectation-Plus Effort means less show, more care.
examples.whatToDo: Mathias makes the subtraction in writing. He removes the contest so staff attention can go to scoring help and a cleaner handoff.
examples.whyItMatters: Expectation-plus is not piling on every nice idea. It often means cutting one demand so the extra care lands where it helps.

examples.title: Pledge Repair Split
examples.scenario: The Sunday fundraiser pledge was saved, but only volunteer Sarah's apology got answered. Sebastien found the wrong total on the pledge sheet, corrected the receipt, and sent the note needed to meet expectations before leaving the place of worship pew where volunteers counted cash. Sarah found the same error, stayed after the pews emptied, called the donor, and gave a clear next step. Expectation-Plus Effort made exceed expectations visible.
examples.whatToDo: Sarah keeps the correction human after the paperwork is right. Sebastien meets the baseline; Sarah adds the call and next step.
examples.whyItMatters: Both responses are competent. Acceleration asks where added thought or care can multiply the effect of work that already meets the standard.

questions.prompt: Your team has shipped the basic update, and the last review shows room for one careful pass. Which next move fits acceleration?
choices: Spend one extra pass on the part that can change the result.
Send the normal version now because the baseline promise was already met.
Trim the review step because acceleration should make the update easier to finish.
questions.explanation: Acceleration adds energy or thought at the margin. Sending the baseline may be competent, and trimming care misreads acceleration as less effort.

questions.prompt: A runner reaches the hill where he usually walks, with yesterday's easy miles behind him. Which reading uses Obstacle Leverage well?
choices: The hill shows his training system has stopped working for this route today.
The hill means he should save effort until the route feels smooth again.
The hill is the spot where staying with the plan can create growth.
questions.explanation: Obstacle Leverage reads the hard point as the growth point. Treating the hill as system failure sends him away from the exact test.

questions.prompt: You finish an easy month of practice, then the first rough week arrives. What should you remember about the easy stretch?
choices: It built the capacity you need now that the work is harder.
It was the whole purpose of the system, so pressure ends the run.
It proved hard weeks should wait until the streak feels clean.
questions.explanation: The easy period is a warm-up. It builds capacity for pressure; it is not the whole aim or proof that hard weeks should be avoided.

questions.prompt: A sales lead says top performers must not face the same follow-up stalls as everyone else. What correction fits the unit?
choices: Top performers avoid common stalls because better systems remove them before follow-up slows.
Many people meet similar stalls; the split comes from who keeps going.
Shared stalls matter less than choosing work with fewer barriers to manage.
questions.explanation: The split is response, not freedom from ordinary barriers. The unit says many people face similar limits, and some continue through them.

questions.prompt: During a hard gym set, a lifter reaches the end of strict form while the bar still moves a little. Which move fits the Arnold example?
choices: End the set at the first form limit so the plateau stays clean.
Change the exercise early so the hard portion does not arrive.
Adjust technique after the limit so more muscles help extend the set.
questions.explanation: Arnold's example uses an adjustment after the weight-lifting limit. Ending at once or changing early misses the after-limit move.

questions.prompt: During a plateau review, a coach says a small technique change cannot add much after strict form stops. Which detail checks that claim?
choices: The adjustment mainly kept the set smoother at the same count today.
The adjustment added five to six reps after the strict-form stop.
The adjustment replaced the set with a shorter lift before strain.
questions.explanation: The grounded detail is five to six extra reps. The example is not same-count smoothing or replacing the hard set before strain.

questions.prompt: A designer wants to skip user testing and calls it a smart detour. Which test separates detour from shortcut?
choices: It counts as a detour if it makes the work easier to describe to stakeholders.
It helps after prior effort hits a real barrier and keeps work moving.
It counts as a shortcut when the team has already named the goal.
questions.explanation: A smart detour sustains effort after a real barrier. Skipping testing before the barrier avoids work instead of extending it.

questions.prompt: You delivered the promised repair and still have one useful customer note you could add. What does expectation-plus ask?
choices: Add the note when it gives value beyond the baseline promise.
Hold the note because meeting the promise is the upper target.
Replace the repair with the note so extra effort is more visible.
questions.explanation: Expectation-plus means added value beyond the expected baseline. Holding at the baseline misses the accelerator; replacing the repair skips competence.

questions.prompt: A teammate repeats the average response at every rough edge and expects unusual results later. Which critique fits acceleration?
choices: The average response works if it is repeated long enough under pressure.
The rough edge should wait until the team feels ready to return.
Unusual results require behavior that differs when pressure rises.
questions.explanation: Acceleration asks for behavior outside the average response when limits appear. Repeating the usual stop is not enough for unusual results.

reviewCards.front: What does acceleration at limits ask you to do when momentum hits a wall?
reviewCards.back: Add a smart push after real effort has reached a barrier. The push may be more energy, a better use of the obstacle, or care beyond the expected baseline.

reviewCards.front: Why are easy periods called the warm-up for acceleration?
reviewCards.back: Easy streaks build capacity. They matter because the harder moment will test whether the routine can keep working when effort is no longer smooth.

reviewCards.front: How do Arnold Schwarzenegger's cheat reps show the difference between detour and shortcut?
reviewCards.back: He adjusted technique after hitting a weight-lifting limit, so more muscle groups could extend the set. The detour kept work going after the wall.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate behavioral momentum (Ch 4), then use it on acceleration at limits?
reviewCards.back: Behavioral momentum is the force that comes from repeated action becoming normal. Acceleration uses that stored rhythm at the hard spot, where the next push now has something behind it.

reviewCards.front: What makes Expectation-Plus Effort different from simply meeting the bar?
reviewCards.back: Meeting the bar fulfills the baseline. Expectation-plus adds useful thought or care after the baseline is safe, so competent work has a larger effect.

reviewCards.front: What are the 3 acceleration levers named in this unit?
reviewCards.back: They are extra energy, obstacle leverage, and expectation-plus. Each one asks for more useful effort at the margin, not an easier way around the work.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice finding the hard spot where momentum starts to stall. Use Cut One Demand at the Wall: remove one lesser task, option, or flourish so extra energy can go to the part that changes the result. Then choose the lever that fits: extra energy, obstacle leverage, or expectation-plus.

ifThenPlans.context: A familiar obstacle makes the plan feel broken.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the wall makes the plan feel broken, then Cut One Demand at the Wall. Remove one low-value demand and use the freed effort on the next real move.

ifThenPlans.context: A workaround starts to sound like relief from the work.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the workaround appears before real effort reaches a barrier, then Cut One Demand at the Wall. Keep the work and remove only the extra demand.

ifThenPlans.context: The baseline is met, but one extra act of care would help.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the baseline is safe and the extra care has a clear receiver, then Cut One Demand at the Wall. Drop one flourish and fund expectation-plus.

ifThenPlans.context: The average response would stop at the rough edge.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the average response is to stop, then Cut One Demand at the Wall. Choose one behavior that differs under pressure and do that first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next day, use your laptop lid as the cue. When you close it between tasks, write one demand to remove and one extra-care move for the next hard spot.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of the week, review once and name what changed about Cut One Demand at the Wall: what you removed, where you added effort, and what result shifted. Do not keep a daily log.

memorableLines.text: The hard spot is the hinge.
A detour is honest when it keeps you working.
